rationale: Abnormal clinical EEG shows up as diffuse or focal slowing, too much or too little amplitude, and changed fast activity, so I'm replacing the 5 relative bands with a finer log spectrum. Each channel gets absolute log power in 2-Hz bins (1–45 Hz) plus log total power; relative power is a linear function of these features, so the model can still recover it. Because this adds many features, the regularization strength C is now picked by grouped inner CV on the training fold only.

The current model only sees per-channel power, so it misses abnormal spatial structure such as focal slowing, asymmetries and changes in how channels relate to each other. This change adds band-limited covariance matrices in 5 bands (delta/theta/alpha/beta/gamma), mapped to Riemannian tangent space using a reference point fitted on the training fold only. They are appended to the current log spectrum and fed to the same inner-CV-tuned L2 logistic regression.

Many clinical abnormalities in TUAB come and go: intermittent focal or diffuse slowing, epileptiform bursts, and episodes of drowsiness or arousal. A 5-minute Welch average and a single covariance matrix blur these out. This change adds per-channel temporal variability of log band power, measured across non-overlapping 4-s epochs in 5 bands: the standard deviation and the 90th-percentile-minus-median spread, which picks up bursts. These are appended to the existing log spectrum and tangent-space covariances, and fed to the same inner-CV-tuned L2 logistic regression.

I'm adding a gradient-boosted tree model alongside the existing logistic regression and averaging their rank-normalized predictions. Clinical abnormality probably depends on non-additive feature combinations that a linear model can't capture, for example how much slow-wave power is abnormal depends on overall amplitude and on how well the posterior alpha rhythm is organized; the trees can pick these up while the regularized linear model keeps the ensemble stable. The trees are trained on the same log-spectrum and tangent-space covariance features with fixed, conservative settings: shallow trees, strong subsampling and a low learning rate.

TUH clinical recordings carry no artifact rejection, so electrode pops, movement bursts, clipped (±800 µV) stretches and flat segments currently go straight into the Welch mean and the covariance estimates. I'm adding robust segment rejection. Each 4-s Welch segment (50% overlap) is dropped if its channel-averaged log broadband power is more than 3.5 robust z-scores (median/MAD) from the recording's typical value, or if it contains clipped samples, with at most 50% of segments dropped. The log spectrum and the band covariances are then computed only from the kept data. The aim is cleaner estimates of the underlying background rhythm, which carries the abnormality signal. I have not run this; its Dev score is unknown.

Power spectra and covariance matrices ignore phase, so they miss waveform shape. Clinical abnormalities such as sharp waves, spikes and arciform or sharply contoured slow activity show up in the shape of the waves. This change adds per-channel higher-order statistics of the clean 1–45 Hz signal: median per-segment skewness, log kurtosis and skewness of the derivative (rise vs. fall asymmetry), plus the Higuchi fractal dimension. They are appended to the existing features for the same LR+LightGBM ensemble.

The covariance bands are coarse, so I'm splitting them into 9 narrower physiological sub-bands: 1–2.5, 2.5–4, 4–6, 6–8, 8–10, 10–13, 13–20, 20–30 and 30–45 Hz. Abnormal EEG findings have different spatial patterns in different sub-bands, for example focal polymorphic delta vs. intermittent rhythmic delta, drowsy theta vs. slowed posterior rhythm, and low vs. high alpha. The current 5 bands average these patterns together.

Two key clinical signs of an abnormal EEG are a slowed or missing posterior dominant rhythm and a changed background slope. The current 2-Hz bins can't resolve the first and only capture the second indirectly. This change adds a FOOOF-style parameterization of each channel's clean spectrum (0.25 Hz resolution). It fits a log-log aperiodic line over 2–40 Hz, leaving out 6–14 Hz, which gives an offset and an exponent. From what's left after removing that line in 4–14 Hz, it takes the peak frequency, the peak height and the centroid.

TUH neurologists read these recordings in the longitudinal bipolar "double banana" (TCP) montage because it cancels diffuse activity and brings out focal slowing and other local abnormalities. Our current features are average-reference log spectra plus tangent-space covariances, and neither contains per-pair log power in fine frequency bins. This change adds a fine log spectrum (2-Hz bins from 1 to 45 Hz, plus log total power) for the 18 standard bipolar derivations. It is computed from the same artifact-free segments and feeds the same LR+LightGBM ensemble. I have not run it, so its Dev score is unknown.

Adding the LightGBM model in round 4 gave the biggest gain from a model change so far. In rounds 3, 6, 8 and 9, adding more features slightly lowered the score, so this round changes the model instead. I'm adding a CatBoost model alongside LightGBM, trained on the same features. CatBoost's symmetric trees and ordered boosting tend to overfit less when there are few samples and many correlated tangent-space features. I expect averaging the two tree models to give a less noisy nonlinear part. The final score weights the predictions 50/50 between the linear model and the trees, as before.

TUAB recordings switch between eyes open and eyes closed, drowsiness and arousal, so some features change within a recording because of brain state rather than abnormality. Each recording now also gets 3 contiguous ~100-s crops, each with its own artifact-cleaned log spectrum and 9-band covariances. Both models train on the full view plus the crops, with crops grouped by patient in the inner CV, and test predictions are averaged over the views. The aim is to make the models down-weight state-dependent features in favour of stable, trait-like ones, and to quadruple the effective training data for the ~2,150-feature model.

Adding feature families has kept failing (rounds 3, 6, 8, 9), and a second tree model (CatBoost, round 10) added almost nothing. This change adds a third, different kind of model instead: a small regularized neural net. It is an MLP on the same standardized log-spectrum and tangent-space features, with input and hidden dropout and weight decay, averaged over 3 seeds and trained on all crop views. It can learn smooth nonlinear interactions, for example between diffuse slowing, overall amplitude and how organized the spatial covariance is. Its errors should overlap less with the linear model and the trees than another tree model's would. The three models are rank-averaged with equal weight. I have not run this, so its Dev score is unknown.

LightGBM is still fixed at 600 trees with learning rate 0.03. That setting was picked before crop augmentation quadrupled the training rows, so it may now stop too early or run too long. This change picks the number of boosting rounds by early stopping on a held-out set of patients from the training fold (the first grouped inner fold, scored by AUC). It then refits on the whole training fold with that number of rounds, scaled up by 1.25 because the refit has about 25% more data. I have not run it, so its effect on the Dev score is unknown.

Crop augmentation (round 11) was the latest kept gain, and its premise was that more within-recording brain-state variability teaches the models to rely on stable, trait-like abnormality features. This change raises the crops per recording from 3 disjoint ~100-s windows to 5 overlapping ones. Each crop is still 1/3 of the recording (stride 1/6), so each crop's estimates are no noisier than before. Training gets more state-mixed views, and test predictions average over 6 views instead of 4. I have not run it, so the Dev score is unknown, and the extra views will also make each CV run slower.

LightGBM splits on one feature at a time, so it cannot easily form differences such as "slow-band power relative to total power" or "whole-head spectral shape". These are the quantities that describe diffuse slowing and a poorly organized background. This change gives only the tree model explicit per-channel log relative spectra (log bin minus log total) and channel-averaged log absolute and relative spectra. The logistic regression is unchanged, because for it these extras would just repeat linear combinations it can already form.

The data are average-referenced, so every band covariance is rank-deficient: its eigenvalue along the all-ones direction is roughly zero. Right now 1% trace shrinkage is mixed into all eigenvalues to make the matrices invertible. That shrinkage distorts the small eigen-directions (especially in the low-power beta and gamma bands), and the tangent space then includes a degenerate, mostly constant log-eigenvalue. This change projects each covariance onto the orthonormal (n−1)-dimensional complement of the ones vector, where the matrices are full rank. It then uses only a tiny ridge (0.1%), so the Riemannian tangent features reflect the actual spatial structure of each sub-band, in line with rank-aware Riemannian pipelines for clinical EEG.

Whether a recording is abnormal does not depend on which side the abnormality is on: left focal slowing is as abnormal as right. I'm adding a label-preserving left-right mirror augmentation, which swaps homologous 10-20 channels in the spectra and permutes each projected covariance exactly (C' = Q C Qᵀ with the orthogonal Q = Bᵀ P B). Training then uses both the original and the mirrored views, grouped by patient, and test predictions are averaged over the original and mirrored views. Like the kept crop augmentation, this doubles the effective data for the ~2,000-feature models and builds in a hemispheric-symmetry prior. I have not run it, so the Dev score is unknown, and 8 views per recording instead of 4 will make each CV run slower against the ~25-minute limit.

The log spectrum currently averages the power of the kept 4-s segments, so a few high-power stretches can dominate it: eye movements in frontal delta, muscle in beta and gamma, transient arousals. The background rhythm is what carries the abnormality signal, so I replace the mean with a per-channel, per-bin median over the kept segments (and the same for total power). This gives a more robust background estimate without adding any features.

In round 18, taking the median spectrum over segments made the log spectrum robust to transients, but the band covariances still use the arithmetic mean over all clean samples, so high-power bursts dominate them. This change computes one projected covariance per kept 4-s segment and combines them with the log-Euclidean (geometric) mean, per view and per sub-band. That damps transient high-power epochs and gives a geometry-consistent estimate of the background spatial structure, without adding any features.

This retries the round-19 idea, which timed out, in a form that should run fast enough. Each projected sub-band covariance becomes the log-Euclidean (geometric) mean of covariances from non-overlapping 16-s blocks, using only artifact-free samples, so transient high-power bursts no longer dominate the spatial-structure estimate the way they do in the arithmetic mean. To keep it fast and numerically sound, each band is projected once and all block covariances are computed in one batched step. The 16-s blocks give enough degrees of freedom even in the 1–2.5 Hz band (4-s blocks would be rank-deficient), and the matrix logs are computed once per block and shared by all crop views. I haven't run this, so the timeout fix and the Dev score are both unverified.
